F27.quote: libcom.org is a resource for all people who wish to fight to improve their lives, their communities and their working conditions. We want to discuss, learn from successes and failures of the past and develop strategies to increase the power we, as ordinary people, have over our own lives.
F27.claim: libcom.org defines itself as a resource for people who fight to improve their lives, communities and working conditions, to learn from the successes and failures of the past
F27.lineage: libcom.org: what the site says it is

F28.quote: Author libcom.org Submitted by libcom on September 11, 2006
F28.claim: the introduction is authored by libcom.org and dated 11 September 2006

F29.quote: Every day, ordinary people are fighting back. Workers organise , strike , occupy and revolt , standing up for human needs in an inhuman world. This site is for them. You. Us.
F29.claim: the site is for workers who organise, strike, occupy and revolt
F29.lineage: libcom.org: what the site says it is

F30.quote: The name libcom is an abbreviation of "libertarian communism", the political idea we identify with.
F30.claim: the name abbreviates 'libertarian communism', the political idea it identifies with

F31.quote: We are also influenced by certain specific theoretical and practical traditions, such as anarchist-communism , anarcho-syndicalism , Autonomist Marxism , black liberation , council communism , feminism , ultra-left Marxism , and others.
F31.claim: the traditions it names as influences: anarchist-communism, anarcho-syndicalism, Autonomist Marxism, black liberation, council communism, feminism, ultra-left Marxism

F32.quote: We have sympathies with writers and organisations including Karl Marx , CLR James , Rosa Luxemburg , Maurice Brinton , Mariarosa dalla Costa , Ambalavaner Sivanandan , Martin Glaberman , Anton Pannekoek
F32.claim: the writers it names as sympathies, Marx, CLR James, Luxemburg, Brinton, Pannekoek among them

F33.quote: However, we recognise the limitations of applying these ideas and organisational forms to contemporary society.
F33.claim: its stated limit: the ideas and organisational forms it draws on have limits when applied to contemporary society

F34.quote: The site contains news and analysis of workers' struggles, discussions and a constantly growing archive of over 20,000 articles contributed by our 10,000+ users ranging from history and biographies to theoretical texts, complete books and pamphlets.
F34.claim: an archive of over 20,000 articles contributed by over 10,000 users, from history and biographies to theory, books and pamphlets

F35.quote: We have incorporated several other online archives over the years, and in addition have hundreds of exclusive texts written or scanned by or for us.
F35.claim: it has incorporated other online archives and holds hundreds of texts written or scanned for it

F36.quote: We are completely independent of all trade unions and political parties; the site is funded entirely by subs from our volunteer administrators and donations from users .
F36.claim: independent of all trade unions and parties; funded by its volunteer administrators' subs and users' donations

F37.quote: Libcom.org is an online platform featuring a variety of libertarian communist essays, blog posts, and archives, primarily in English.
F37.claim: Wikipedia: an online platform of libertarian communist essays, blog posts and archives, primarily in English

F38.quote: It was founded in 2005 by editors in the United States and the United Kingdom .
F38.claim: Wikipedia: founded in 2005 by editors in the United States and the United Kingdom

marks.internally_inconsistent: Wikipedia states the founding two ways: lead s2 'founded in 2005' (F38) and History ¶1 'launched in 2003 originally as enrager.net … changed its name in 2005' (F41); both carried

F39.quote: Libcom.org also has a forum and social media features including the ability to comment on post and upload original articles.
F39.claim: Wikipedia: a forum, comments and uploading of original articles (Croeser 2018)

F40.quote: In contrast with traditional archives, anarchistic archival practices embrace "use as preservation", making use of digital technology to host niche political material in online repositories like Libcom.org.
F40.claim: Wikipedia, after Cornell 2019: anarchist archival practice is 'use as preservation', with online repositories such as Libcom.org hosting niche political material

F41.quote: The site was launched in 2003 originally as enrager.net , named for the enragés of the French Revolution , but changed its name in 2005 to the present name libcom.org, short for libertarian communism.
F41.claim: launched in 2003 as enrager.net, after the enragés, renamed libcom.org in 2005

marks.internally_inconsistent: see F38: the same article gives 2005 as the founding and 2003 as the launch under the earlier name; both carried

F42.quote: The enrager.net web collective was a splinter of the London group inside the Anarchist Youth Network, an organization founded in 2002 by two members of the Anarchist Federation .
F42.claim: the enrager.net collective split from the London group of the Anarchist Youth Network

F43.claim: Wikipedia's infobox gives the content licence as Creative Commons BY-NC-SA 2.5, citing the site's legal notes (accessed 2021-04-11)

F44.quote: Since then, we believe it has grown to be the world's most popular English-language anarchist/libertarian socialist website, with over 15,000 texts, over 6000 contributing users
F44.claim: Wikipedia's reference quotes the site's 2013 post: over 15,000 texts and over 6,000 contributing users
